\begin{document}

\noindent\textbf{Setup in six lines.} The task is two-number arithmetic posed in words
(\texttt{What is the sum of 621 and 5068?}, answered 0-shot); the same problems can be posed in
symbols (\texttt{621 + 5068 = }), the ``symbol surface''. The model is TinyStories-1B (16
layers, 32 heads per layer, width 2048), pretrained on children's stories with no arithmetic.
Five parents are fine-tuned on the word task: the \emph{elicit parent} (TS1B-latent: the base
plus symbol arithmetic plus a word$\leftrightarrow$symbol binding, so the capability is present
but never shown on the task); the \emph{symbol engine} (the base plus symbol arithmetic only, no
binding); the \emph{format-installed} parent (the base taught only to emit a number in the right
format, no arithmetic); the \emph{blank} base; and Llama-3.2-1B, an off-the-shelf second elicit
parent used in the parent-only metrics. \emph{Elicit} $=$ fine-tune the elicit parent;
\emph{teach} $=$ fine-tune the format-installed parent (the blank base is the control). Two
methods: full FT updates every weight; LoRA trains rank-512 adapters on frozen weights. Metrics
marked $\bigstar$ need only the parent and are measured on all five parents (Table~\ref{tab:prefit}).

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{llllccc}
\toprule
endpoint & parent & method & data & steps (passes) & stop & exact match \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicit FT} & TS1B-latent & full FT & 4M & 21{,}500 (0.7) & converged & \textbf{0.986} \\
\textbf{teach FT} & format-installed & full FT & 4M & 58{,}500 (1.9) & converged & \textbf{0.424} \\
\midrule
elicit LoRA (sweep, snapshots) & TS1B-latent & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 1M & 11{,}500 (1.5) & converged & 0.981 \\
teach LoRA (sweep) & format-installed & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 1M & -- & converged & 0.079 \\
teach LoRA (snapshots) & blank & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 1M & 25{,}000 (3.2) & converged & 0.093 \\
teach LoRA 4M (control) & blank & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 4M & 39{,}500 (1.3) & converged & 0.139 \\
teach FT from the blank base (control) & blank & full FT & 4M & 72{,}000 (2.3) & converged & 0.819 \\
\bottomrule

\caption{The main pair (top) and the endpoints used where noted (bottom). LoRA learning rate

% =====================================================================


\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{M\arabic*}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=1.2em, resume]

\metricsec{Circuit overlap}{the same circuit vs.\ a new circuit}
\what{Does the fine-tuned model solve the task with the circuit its parent already had (elicit)
or with a circuit that did not exist before (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item \emph{Nodes.} The model is cut into 528 parts: 512 attention heads and 16 MLP blocks.
\item \emph{Scoring.} For each node, how much the answer's logit would move if that node's
activation were swapped for its value on a different problem (first-order estimate: activation
difference $\times$ gradient), averaged over 128--256 problem pairs. The top 32 are the circuit.
\item \emph{Comparing.} Jaccard@32 $=$ shared nodes $\div$ union. Read against two references:
the \emph{ceiling} (split-half), the overlap of the same model's circuit built from two halves
of the data (how repeatable a circuit is at all), and the \emph{type-matched chance}, what two
unrelated circuits with the same MLP/head mix share (0.20--0.27 here).
\item \emph{Heads only.} The same overlap over the 512 heads alone, where circuits can actually
differ (chance 0.03).
\item \emph{Edges.} The same scoring for the connections between nodes (which node's output
each node reads, $\approx$8.4K edges); the 256 strongest are the wiring, compared the same way.
\item \emph{Functional check.} Overlap counts names; this counts effect. Corrupt a set of 32
heads (write in their activations from a different problem) and read how much of the model's
answer preference is destroyed, against random sets of 32 heads. A set identified on the
\emph{parent} and evaluated in the \emph{child} tests reuse without depending on which names
rank highest.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:overlap}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit:} parent $\leftrightarrow$ child $0.455$ (chance $0.23$, ceilings $0.60$ /
$0.56$); heads only $0.333$ against the parent's own ceiling of $0.42$; wiring $0.358$ against
ceilings of $0.49$ / $0.51$ --- the child keeps the parent's connections about as much as its
nodes (edge change only $1.3\times$ node change after ceiling correction). \textbf{Teach:} the
parent has no circuit for the task (its node-score map is noise, M10), so the child's is new;
heads only $0.016$.
\item Functional check: the parent's 32 heads, found before any target training, carry
$0.73$ of the elicited child's behaviour (random heads $0.04$; the child's own top heads
$0.88$). The taught child's own top heads carry only $0.46$ of its behaviour, and $0.27$ of
the elicited child's: teaching layers diffuse attention on the shared number-reading heads (M2)
instead of inheriting a compact head circuit. Set overlap between the two children is at chance
($0.306$; heads only $0.103$).
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Comparison & Jaccard@32 & type-matched chance & ceilings (A / B) & heads-only J@32 \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicit parent $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child} & \textbf{0.455} & 0.23 & 0.600 / 0.561 & \textbf{0.333} (ceiling 0.42) \\
\textbf{teach parent $\leftrightarrow$ taught child} & \textbf{undefined} (parent map is noise; 0.231) & 0.25 & -- / 0.524 & \textbf{0.016} \\
\midrule
elicit parent on the task $\leftrightarrow$ on symbols & 0.524 & 0.27 & 0.600 / 0.306 & 0.280 \\
elicit parent on symbols $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child & 0.391 & 0.25 & 0.306 / 0.561 & 0.255 \\
elicited child, full FT $\leftrightarrow$ LoRA & 0.641 & 0.20 & 0.561 / 0.684 & 0.455 \\
elicited child $\leftrightarrow$ taught child & 0.306 & 0.25 & 0.561 / 0.524 & 0.103 \\
taught child $\leftrightarrow$ taught child from the blank base & 0.362 & 0.27 & 0.524 / 0.422 & 0.208 \\
\midrule
wiring (256 edges): elicit parent $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child & 0.358 & 0.03 & 0.493 / 0.510 & -- \\
wiring (256 edges): elicited child $\leftrightarrow$ taught child & 0.267 & 0.03 & 0.510 / 0.446 & -- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Circuit overlaps of the full-FT children and their parents, mapped on the word task
(0-shot). Uniform chance is $0.031$ everywhere; ceilings are each map's own split-half
repeatability; the teach parent's map fails the performing check (logit-diff $-1.5$ nats, M11),
so its overlap is noise. Wiring rows: Jaccard over the 256 strongest edges, each map's own
split-half ceiling; edges change $1.3\times$ as much as nodes under elicitation here (Llama
base$\to$fine-tune: $2.2\times$).
Bottom: the elicit parent's task circuit is its symbol-arithmetic circuit; the elicited circuit
is method-independent; the two children against each other; two taught circuits against each
other.}
\label{tab:overlap}
\end{table}

\metricsec{Head roles}{the same reader heads vs.\ rediscovered ones}
\what{Does the fine-tuned model keep the parent's heads that read the two numbers (elicit) or
have to find reader heads of its own (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Take a problem and a twin that differs in one thing only (a different first number).
\item Learn the smallest set of attention heads such that copying their activations from the
twin makes the model answer the twin's problem (Desiderata Component Masking, Prakash et al.\
2024). Those heads carry that piece of information.
\item A set counts only if it flips the answer as often as copying every head does (the
ceiling). Sets are compared across models by Jaccard (chance $\approx0.05$).
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:dcm}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit:} the child's number-reading heads are the parent's, $0.69$ / $0.86$
(first / second number; reference sets $=$ the elicit parent on symbols). \textbf{Teach}
(against the same reference, since the teach parent has no reader heads, M14): the child finds
a larger set that still contains most of the same heads, $0.88$ / $0.66$ --- a graded
difference, not an absence.
\item A taught model that never learned the task has no compact set at all.
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Comparison (first operand / second operand) & $|A|$ & $|B|$ & Jaccard & flip acc.\ / ceiling of $A$ \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicited child (FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicit parent on symbols} & 31 / 25 & 30 / 27 & \textbf{0.694 / 0.857} & 0.98 / 0.98 (at ceiling) \\
\textbf{taught child (FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicit parent on symbols} & 32 / 41 & 30 / 27 & \textbf{0.879 / 0.659} & 0.59 / 0.54 (0.59 / 0.55) \\
taught child (FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (LoRA) & 32 / 41 & 36 / 30 & 0.659 / 0.690 & -- \\
\midrule
elicit parent on symbols $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (LoRA), symbol surface & 30 / 27 & 32 / 30 & 0.879 / 0.900 & at ceiling \\
elicit parent on symbols $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (LoRA), operation role & 25 & 24 & 0.750 & at ceiling \\
elicited child (FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (LoRA) & 31 / 25 & 36 / 30 & 0.811 / 0.833 & 0.98 / 0.98 \\
taught child that did not learn (LoRA 4M) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (LoRA) & 12 / 21 & 36 / 30 & 0.043 / 0.041 & 0.01 / 0.03 (0.20 / 0.14) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Head roles by Desiderata Component Masking. Reference role sets $=$ the elicit parent
on the symbol surface, where it already answers. $|A|$, $|B|$ $=$ size of the two role sets. Bottom: the
references (the LoRA-elicited child keeps the parent's roles almost exactly; a taught model that
never learned the task has no roles to compare).}
\label{tab:dcm}
\end{table}

\metricsec{Circuit formation time}{present at step 1 vs.\ assembled mid-run}
\what{Is the final circuit present from the first step (elicit) or assembled somewhere in the
middle of training (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Snapshots were saved along the LoRA runs (128 per run); the full-FT runs have none, so
this metric uses the two 1M LoRA runs (Table~\ref{tab:endpoints}: elicit LoRA and teach LoRA from the blank base).
\item At each snapshot, build the circuit as in M1 and take its overlap with the run's final
circuit. The circuit exists once the curve leaves chance; it is finished once it reaches the
ceiling.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Figure~\ref{fig:form}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit:} $0.49$ overlap with the final circuit at step 1 ($16\times$ chance),
locked from step 1.5K of 11.5K. \textbf{Teach:} at chance until step 1.3K, built over steps
1.3K--5.4K of 25K --- the stretch where its loss on new examples drops fastest.
\end{steps}}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_formation_ts.png}
\caption{Circuit formation, elicit (left) vs teach (right); dashed = split-half ceiling.}
\label{fig:form}
\end{figure}

\metricsec{Gradient pressure}{a dying gradient vs.\ a growing one}
\what{Does the gradient fade as training proceeds because there is nothing left to change
(elicit), or grow because structure is still being built (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item The size of the gradient (before clipping) at every training step.
\item Compare its average over the first 1\% of steps with the last 10\%: a ratio above 1 means
the gradient fades, below 1 means it grows. Also the total gradient accumulated over the run.
\item Norms are comparable within one fine-tuning method only.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:grad}, Figure~\ref{fig:grad}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit:} fades $3.4\times$ from the first 1\% to the last 10\%. \textbf{Teach:}
grows $1.4\times$, and accumulates $8.6\times$ the total gradient ($378$K vs $44$K).
\item Under LoRA the gap is larger ($40\times$ growth, $150\times$ the mass), aimed at attention
weights --- the number-reading heads of M2 being written. Figure~\ref{fig:grad} repeats both
quantities across the sweep over training-set size $n$.
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & \textbf{elicit FT} & \textbf{teach FT} & elicit LoRA 1M & teach LoRA 1M (blank) \\
\midrule
steps & 21{,}500 & 58{,}500 & 11{,}500 & 25{,}000 \\
peak gradient norm (step) & 34.0 (1) & 70.9 (50{,}860) & 0.441 (96) & 17.4 (23{,}657) \\
mean norm: first 1\% / middle / last 10\% & 4.80 / 1.85 / 1.39 & 2.69 / 4.86 / 3.77 & 0.183 / 0.060 / 0.056 & 0.169 / 5.21 / 6.80 \\
first 1\% $\div$ last 10\% & $\times$3.4 (decays) & $\times$0.7 (grows 1.4$\times$) & $\times$3.3 (decays) & $\times$0.02 (grows $\sim$40$\times$) \\
cumulative gradient mass $\sum_t\|g_t\|$ & 44{,}021 & 378{,}170 & 783 & 116{,}877 \\
gradient mass per step & 2.05 & 6.46 & 0.068 & 4.68 \\
mass share QK / VO / MLP & -- & -- & .18 / .55 / .27 & .12 / .87 / .01 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Raw gradient strength (pre-clip global norm at every update). LoRA and full-FT norms are
on different parameter sets and are compared within a method only; the LoRA pair is shown for
the per-class split, which the full-FT trainer does not log.}
\label{tab:grad}
\end{table}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_grad_strength.png}
\caption{Cumulative gradient mass (left) and late-run gradient norm (right) vs $n$; teal = teach, gold = elicit.}
\label{fig:grad}
\end{figure}

\metricsec{Weight write}{a small update vs.\ a large one}
\what{Is the change to the weights small and efficient (elicit) or large and expensive per unit
of capability gained (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Relative weight change $\|\Delta W\|/\|W\|$ between child and parent, over all attention
and MLP matrices.
\item Along the LoRA runs (the only ones with snapshots): total distance the weights travel, and
capability per unit travelled $=$ final exact match $\div$ distance.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:weights}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit} $0.050$ vs \textbf{teach} $0.086$: teaching writes $1.7\times$ more into the
weights.
\item Under LoRA: $3.8\times$ the distance for $40\times$ less capability per unit travelled.
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}

 & elicit & teach \\
\midrule
\textbf{relative write $\|\Delta W\|/\|W\|$, full FT} & \textbf{0.050} & \textbf{0.086} \\
\midrule
relative write, LoRA 1M (teach from the blank base) & 0.095 & 0.212 \\
steps (LoRA 1M) & 11{,}500 & 25{,}000 \\
peak / final writing speed per step (LoRA 1M) & 0.218 / 0.018 & 0.306 / 0.022 \\
total weight travel $\|\Delta W\|_F$ (LoRA 1M) & 120 & 457 \\
final exact match (LoRA 1M) & 0.981 & 0.093 \\
capability per unit travel (LoRA 1M) & $8.1\times10^{-3}$ & $2.0\times10^{-4}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\caption{Weight-space write. Top: the pair. Bottom: the LoRA runs, the only ones with snapshots

\label{tab:weights}

\metricsec{What fine-tuning changes in the internal state}{a different change per problem vs.\ the same change every time}
\what{When the child's internal state is compared with the parent's on the same problem, is the
change different for every problem --- the child has added that problem's answer (elicit) --- or
is it mostly the same change regardless of the problem --- the child has been moved into a new
mode (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item For each of 256 problems, take the model's internal state at the moment it is about to
answer (a 2048-number vector), in the parent and in the child, and subtract. That difference is
``the change'' fine-tuning made on that problem.
\item Ask whether the 256 changes point the same way: the share of their total energy along the
single best direction (\emph{shared-direction score}; 1.0 $=$ the same push every time).
\item Control: recompute after removing the directions that spell the answer token, so ``the
same push'' cannot simply be the answer.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Figure~\ref{fig:resid}, Table~\ref{tab:resid}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit} $0.056$ (each problem's change is its own) vs \textbf{teach} $0.567$
(over half of every change is one shared push), unchanged with the answer removed.
\item The taught child from the blank base, which did have an output format to learn, scores
$0.526$ --- no higher, so the shared push is the algorithm's mode, not ``output a number''.
\end{steps}}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{figures/fig_resid_shift.png}
\caption{The pair (thick) with the blank-base taught control (thin diamonds). Left: relative change
of the internal state by layer at the answer position (solid) and on generic story text
(dashed). Right:
shared-direction score (PC1) of the 256 per-problem changes by layer, with the parent's own states
dotted.}
\label{fig:resid}
\end{figure}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & \textbf{elicit FT} & \textbf{teach FT} & teach FT from the blank base (control) \\
\midrule
final exact match & 0.986 & 0.424 & 0.819 \\
shared-direction score (PC1) of the change, last layer (parent's own states) & \textbf{0.056} (0.23) & \textbf{0.567} (0.99) & 0.526 (0.98) \\
same, after removing answer-token directions & 0.061 & 0.561 & 0.528 \\
cosine of each change to the mean change & 0.23 & 0.80 & 0.74 \\
size of the change relative to the parent's state, last layer & 1.92 & 1.22 & 1.36 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Change of the internal state parent$\to$child at the answer position, 256 problems,
fp32. Under LoRA (1M elicit / 4M teach from the blank base): score 0.063 vs 0.528, unchanged
after removing the answer directions; the LoRA-taught size is $29\times$ (an adapter artefact).}
\label{tab:resid}
\end{table}

\metricsecp{Latent reach}{do the words already reach the machinery?}
\what{Before any target training, does a natural-language question already put the arithmetic
components into a problem-specific state (elicit), or is there nothing for the words to reach
(teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Pose each problem twice, in words (\texttt{What is the sum of 621 and 5068?}) and in
symbols (\texttt{621 + 5068 = }), and record each MLP block's activation at the answer position.
\item \emph{Bridging index:} similarity between the two renderings of the same problem, minus
the similarity between renderings of different problems. Positive $=$ the words put the block
into the state the symbols do.
\item Second check: how alike the parent's own states are across problems (shared-direction
score; $\approx1$ $=$ the same state for every problem).
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:resid}, ``parent's own states''.
\begin{steps}
\item Bridging index of the arithmetic MLPs: $\approx0$ in the symbol engine (no binding),
$+0.07$ to $+0.13$ (layers 7--15) in the elicit parent: the binding is what lets the words in.
\item The elicit parent's states are problem-specific ($0.23$); the teach parent sits in the
same state for every problem ($0.99$; blank base $0.98$).
\end{steps}}
\metricsecp{Answer depth}{the answer already there vs.\ absent; finished one layer earlier vs.\ later}
\what{Is the answer readable from the parent's internal state before it can say it (elicit) or
absent (teach); and after training, is it finished one layer earlier (elicit) or later (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Read the model's intermediate state at each layer as if it were the output. Two lenses
(a third, R, is in Table~\ref{tab:lens}): the \emph{logit lens} (unembed directly) and the
\emph{J-lens} (first transport the state to the final layer with the average Jacobian, then
unembed --- what the state is disposed to make the model say).
\item Per layer: the answer's median rank among 128K vocabulary entries (chance 64K) and the
\emph{logit-diff}, the preference for the correct answer over a mismatched problem's (0 $=$ no
signal). Rank alone can be a number prior; the two are read together.
\item \emph{Settled depth:} the first layer from which the answer stays top-ranked.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Figure~\ref{fig:lens}, Table~\ref{tab:lens}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Before training:} the elicit parent ranks the answer $174$ of 128K and prefers it
by $2.1$ nats while its actual output is a restatement of the question in symbols; the teach
parent ranks it $452$ with logit-diff $0.0$ --- a number, not this number.
\item \textbf{After training:} the elicited child settles at layer 14, the taught child at layer
15.
\end{steps}}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{figures/fig_lens_depth.png}
\caption{J-lens read-out of the answer token by layer: median rank (left, chance 64K) and
logit-diff against a mismatched problem's answer (right). Gold = elicit (parent: squares; child:
diamonds; dotted: the parent on the symbol surface), teal = teach (parent: up-triangles; child:
down-triangles), grey = blank base.}
\label{fig:lens}
\end{figure}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
\toprule
model & surface & own acc (first digit, 256 problems) & rank L12 (logit / J / R) & rank L14 (logit / J / R) & read-out & ld \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicit parent} & NL & 0.047 & 5{,}704 / 2{,}606 / 2{,}730 & 436 / 510 / 424 & 174 & $+2.1$ \\
\textbf{teach parent} (format-installed) & NL & 0.004 & 8{,}394 / 4{,}036 / 5{,}417 & 1{,}106 / 997 / 998 & 452 & $0.0$ \\
\textbf{elicited child} (FT) & NL & 0.988 & 1{,}797 / 338 / 492 & 1 / 1 / 1 & 1 & $+18.7$ \\
\textbf{taught child} (FT) & NL & 0.535 & 23{,}909 / 27{,}044 / 25{,}529 & 381 / 961 / 1{,}848 & 1 & $+14.2$ \\
\midrule
blank base & NL & 0.000 & 76{,}049 / 80{,}840 / 78{,}243 & 77{,}707 / 77{,}320 / 79{,}116 & 75{,}441 & $0.0$ \\
taught child from the blank base (FT) & NL & 0.844 & 18{,}988 / 4{,}123 / 9{,}620 & 170 / 138 / 459 & 1 & $+16.1$ \\
elicit parent & symbols & 0.836 & 1{,}224 / 122 / 334 & 1 / 1 / 1 & 1 & $+15.1$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\caption{Median rank of the answer's first digit token among 128K entries under the three lenses;
``own acc'' $=$ the model's own first-digit-token accuracy on the 256 problems; read-out $=$ the
last layer, where all lenses equal the model's output; ld $=$ logit-diff at the read-out (nats).
Bottom: the blank base (rank without a number prior), the taught child from it (settles at layer
15 too), and the elicit parent's own trajectory on symbols, which the elicited child reproduces.}
\label{tab:lens}
\end{table}

\metricsec{Switch-on by patching}{can the capability be turned on without training?}
\what{With the parent's weights frozen, does writing the fine-tuned child's internal activations
into the parent make it solve the task --- possible only if the machinery is already there
(elicit) and impossible if it is not (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Freeze the parent. On each problem, run the fine-tuned child, take its activations at the
32 circuit nodes of M1, and write them into the parent's run at the answer position.
\item Two variants: each problem gets the child's activations on that problem
(\emph{per-prompt}), or every problem gets the child's average activation (\emph{mean vector}).
Control: the same with 32 random nodes.
\item Read exact match; ``format'' $=$ share of outputs that are a number at all.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:steer}, Figure~\ref{fig:ladder}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit:} the child's per-prompt states switch the parent from $0.000$ to $0.121$
(random nodes $0.000$, LoRA donor). \textbf{Teach:} the same patch into the teach parent gives $0.016$.
\item The mean vector changes only the output format: the patch that works is problem-specific.
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Parent (patient) + child (donor), 32 circuit nodes & condition & format & exact match \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicit parent + elicited child's per-prompt states} & circuit nodes & 0.387 & \textbf{0.121} \\
\textbf{teach parent + taught child's per-prompt states} & circuit nodes & 0.836 (parent 1.000) & \textbf{0.016} \\
\midrule
elicit parent + LoRA child's per-prompt states & circuit nodes & 0.359 & 0.125 \\
 & random-32 nodes & 0.051 & 0.000 \\
elicit parent + LoRA child's mean vector & circuit nodes & 0.164 & 0.000 \\
blank base + blank-base taught child's states & every condition & $\le$0.02 & $\le$0.004 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Donor patching, weights frozen. The parents score 0.000 unpatched. Bottom: controls
(random nodes, the mean vector, the LoRA child as donor, the blank-base pair).}
\label{tab:steer}
\end{table}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/fig_intervention_ladder.png}
\caption{Donor patching on the elicit parent (right; left: the same on Llama-3.2-1B, the second
elicit parent of M11--M15), weights frozen except the last bar: unpatched parent, mean vector,
per-prompt states, and the fine-tuned child for scale.}
\label{fig:ladder}
\end{figure}

\metricsecp{Repeatable task circuit in the parent}{a circuit for the task already there vs.\ noise}
\what{Before any target training, does the parent already have a stable set of components that
raise the correct answer's logit on the target task (elicit), or does its attribution map on the
task have no structure at all (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Build the parent's circuit on the target task as in M1, before any target training.
\item \emph{Is it defined?} The tool marks a map as noise when the parent's answer
logit-difference is below 1 nat.
\item \emph{Is it repeatable?} Build it twice from two halves of the problems and take the
overlap.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:parentcirc}.
\begin{steps}
\item \textbf{Elicit parent:} answers nothing, yet has a defined map ($3.1$ nats) that is as
repeatable as a fine-tuned child's, $0.600$ (heads only $0.422$). \textbf{Teach parent:} map
flagged as noise ($-1.5$ nats).
\item The elicit parent's task circuit is its symbol-arithmetic circuit ($0.524$ overlap), the
one the elicited child ends up running (M1).
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
parent, on the target task (0-shot) & exact match & answer logit-diff (nats) & map & split-half Jaccard@32 / 64 / 128 \\
\midrule
\textbf{elicit parent} & 0.000 & $+3.1$ & performing & \textbf{0.600 / 0.580 / 0.552} \\
\textbf{teach parent} (format-installed) & 0.000 & $-1.5$ & noise & -- \\
\midrule
blank base (16-shot) & 0.000 & $-0.3$ & noise & -- \\
elicit parent on the symbol surface & 0.836 & $+11.0$ & performing & 0.306 / 0.333 / 0.399 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{The parent's own task circuit. Chance overlap $0.031$ / $0.065$ / $0.138$. The symbol
surface map is less repeatable than the natural-language one despite a larger logit-difference:
on symbols the parent already answers, and many components carry a little of the signal.}
\label{tab:parentcirc}
\end{table}

\metricsecp{Hidden preference}{prefers the right answer without saying it vs.\ no preference}
\what{Before any target training, does the parent already prefer the correct answer to a wrong
one, even though it never produces it (elicit), or is it indifferent (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item One forward pass per problem, 256 problems, on the parent alone.
\item At the answer position, the logit of the correct answer's first chunk minus the logit of a
different problem's answer. Mean in nats; 0 $=$ no preference.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:prefit}.
\begin{steps}
\item Elicit parent $2.31$, Llama-3.2-1B $1.00$, symbol engine $0.44$, format-installed $0.06$,
blank $0.02$: the order in which the five parents learn the task under fine-tuning (learning
curves not shown here), from parents that produce none of the answers.
\end{steps}}
\metricsecp{Accelerating descent of the task loss}{the drop speeds up along some direction vs.\ tapers along every direction}
\what{Nudge the parent's weights a little: is there a direction in which the task loss drops
faster the further you go --- a capability one push away (elicit) --- or does the drop taper off
whichever way you move (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Take the task loss at the parent's weights and find the two ends of its curvature
spectrum (Hessian-vector products, power iteration, 16 problems).
\item The second derivative along a direction says what happens to the rate of descent:
positive $=$ the drop tapers, negative $=$ it accelerates. $\lambda_{\max}$ and $\lambda_{\min}$
are the strongest taper and the strongest acceleration. \emph{Negative share}
$=-\lambda_{\min}/(\lambda_{\max}-\lambda_{\min})$: the fraction of that range on the
accelerating side, 1 when every strong direction accelerates, 0 when none does. A ratio, so
models of different loss scale compare.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:prefit}.
\begin{steps}
\item Elicit parent $1.00$, Llama-3.2-1B $0.64$, symbol engine $0.48$, format-installed $0.00$,
blank $0.00$: again the order in which they learn. For an elicit parent there is a direction along which
the loss falls faster and faster; for a teach parent every descent tapers off.
\end{steps}}
\metricsecp{Answer carried by the state}{swapping the state moves the answer vs.\ nothing moves}
\what{Does the parent's state at the answer position already carry the answer causally --- swap
it between two problems and the preference follows (elicit) --- or does swapping it change
nothing (teach)?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Take two problems of equal length. Run the parent on the first while overwriting its
state at the answer position, after layer $L$, with the state from the second (whole state, or a
learned $k$-dimensional part of it; Distributed Alignment Search, Geiger et al.\ 2024).
\item Count how often the parent now prefers the second problem's answer. Controls: no swap, and
a random subspace of the same size. 128 test pairs.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:prefit}.
\begin{steps}
\item Swapping the whole state moves the preference by $+0.39$ (elicit parent), $+0.26$ (Llama),
$+0.30$ (symbol engine) against $+0.05$ and $+0.02$ for the teach parents: every parent that can
compute already holds the answer in its state.
\item In the elicit parent a learned 64-dimensional part of the state recovers most of the effect
(flip rate $0.64$ vs $0.41$ for a random 64-dimensional subspace).
\end{steps}}
\metricsecp{Number-reading heads}{words already reach the arithmetic vs.\ they do not}
\what{Do the parent's attention heads already fetch the two numbers when the problem is posed in
words (elicit), or not (teach) --- and does having arithmetic suffice?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Head roles (M2) on the frozen parent with the word prompts, with one change: since the
parent never answers, a head set counts when copying it from the twin problem moves the parent's
\emph{preference} toward the twin's answer.
\item Report the size of the set and its flip rate against the copy-every-head ceiling.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:prefit}.
\begin{steps}
\item Elicit parent 22 heads, Llama-3.2-1B 23; symbol engine, format-installed and blank: none.
The engine has the arithmetic (M13; the numbers are present, M15) but no heads carrying them
from the words to it --- this is the metric that separates the two elicit parents from it.
\end{steps}}
\metricsecp{Operands present at the answer position}{the numbers are there vs.\ weakly there}
\what{Is the information the computation needs --- the two numbers --- already readable from the
parent's state at the moment it is about to answer?}
\how{
\begin{steps}
\item Linear probe on the parent's state at the answer position, about 2,000 addition problems,
held-out split.
\item Target: the two numbers, in the helix features language models use for numbers
(Kantamneni \& Tegmark 2025). Report the best layer's $R^2$.
\end{steps}}
\numbers{Table~\ref{tab:prefit}.
\begin{steps}
\item Elicit parent $0.88$, Llama-3.2-1B $0.86$, symbol engine $0.90$ vs format-installed $0.53$, blank
$0.49$: parents that can compute have both numbers at the answer position.
\item The answer itself is not linearly readable in any parent beyond the two numbers
themselves; it is produced downstream, where the lens and the hidden preference find it.
\end{steps}}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{elicit} & between & \multicolumn{2}{c}{teach} \\
 & elicit parent & Llama-3.2-1B & symbol engine & format-installed & blank \\
\midrule
hidden preference (nats) & \textbf{2.31} & \textbf{1.00} & 0.44 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\
curvature: negative share & \textbf{1.00} & \textbf{0.64} & 0.48 & 0.00 & 0.00 \\
answer state swap: flip gain over no swap & \textbf{+0.39} & \textbf{+0.26} & +0.30 & +0.05 & +0.02 \\
number-reading heads (first operand) & \textbf{22} & \textbf{23} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
operands present ($R^2$) & \textbf{0.88} & \textbf{0.86} & 0.90 & 0.53 & 0.49 \\
repeatable task circuit (split-half) & \textbf{0.600} & -- & -- & noise & noise \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\caption{Parent-only metrics on the five parents. The first two order all five as their
learning curves do; the next two split the parents that can compute from those that cannot;
number-reading heads alone separate the two elicit parents from the symbol engine, which has the
arithmetic but not the interface to the words.}
\label{tab:prefit}
\end{table}

\end{enumerate}
